title: Tiny Snakes Cartwheel Away From Danger
paragraphs: What reads like a cartoon gag has now been put on a rigorous footing: a group of diminutive Southeast Asian snakes flees by cartwheeling, and a paper in Current Biology, led by Yosuke Kojima of Toho University in Japan, dissects the mechanics of the manoeuvre in some detail.

Having filmed 13 snakes of the genus Pseudorabdion, collected in Kubah National Park in Malaysia, along a track barely 20 centimetres wide, the team found that every one of them rolled when given a gentle tap, whereas six snakes of the genus Calamaria, enlisted as controls, never left the ground. The gait is built from a repeated "stroke": one flank is whipped earthwards while an arched stretch of the body swings down beside the head, and the animal alternates sides with each cycle. The dividend is a pace some four times that of ordinary slithering, delivered while the head holds a strikingly steady course, a feat of stabilisation that would not look out of place in a camera gimbal.

Yet the findings should not be oversold. The rolling was coaxed out in a laboratory rather than provoked by genuine predators, the sample is modest, and the evolutionary origins of the trick remain a puzzle. Kojima himself is candid about the unanswered questions: "This mode of locomotion may require a lot of energy, but we don't yet know how long the snakes can sustain it."

questions.q: What does the comparison with a camera gimbal suggest?
questions.a: That the snakes keep their heads remarkably steady while the body rotates.

questions.q: Why do the authors' findings call for restraint?
questions.a: The behaviour was induced in a lab, the sample is small and the evolution is unexplained.

questions.q: What is the function of the six Calamaria snakes in the study?
questions.a: They served as controls and never rolled.
